note: Oak Creek, Wis., Feb 1870: hot stone dug from a barrel-sized hole in marsh, sulphurous smell

Barnhart farm, Richhill Twp, Greene Co., Pa., 1870-08-21: B. F. Barnhart saw it fall within ten feet; 31-35 lb stone, hot, sulphur smell (2 independent accounts: Waynesburg Messenger correspondent + a second report)
same event as S91 (Barnhart, Greene Co., Pa., 1870)
Armory Hill, Springfield, Mass., April 1872: stone fell, burst with loud report (one line)
Frankfort St., New York City, Aug 1872: ~10-lb stone fell on the pavement outside a lager-beer saloon, split, hot, sulphur odor; examined by geologists ('oxide of iron and sulphur'; possibly pyrite)
Indianapolis, 1872: 11-lb stone 'which fell during the late meteoric shower' exhibited at the police office
near New London, Ohio, 1873-08-18: heard passing by Mr. Hotchkiss, struck close to him; dug from 12-14 in., hot, broken in two, one piece sent away (4 papers, New London Record)
same event as S145 (New London, Ohio, 1873)
Portland road, Saco, Maine, Oct 1870: Capt. Ira C. Doe saw a meteor fall; stone presented to the York Institute (now Saco Museum) in 1873. Specimen destination named
near Rossville, Kan. (Kansas paper), July 1874: ~2-lb fragment fell, seen by several people, burned grass
Plymouth Hill, Conn., 1874: ball of fire fell; 15-lb round stone 'as if melted' carried home
Knightstown, Ind., 1874-08-03: aerolite broke into three tiny hot pieces
Gonzales/Seguin, Tex., July 1875: exploded meteor scattered mineral pieces
Tyler, Tex., Sept 1875: meteor exploded, pieces gathered; Archaeological Society of Austin asking for specimens
Newfoundland / Northumberland, Pa., June 1876: hot stone a foot in circumference seen descending and found (Sunbury Daily)
Scott St., First Ward, South Bend, Ind., July 1876: fragment of the fireball fell in a citizen's yard; Prof. Wheeler (Univ. of Chicago) to analyze it
Louisville, Ky., 1876-07-18: ~2-lb stone fell in the street after a sharp report (same event as family F47 'Weatherford engine house')
Manchester, Oct 1876: Ed Gallager saw an aerolite fall near his feet and kept it
Ledyard, Conn., Nov 1876: many meteoric stones found after a bright fireball seen from Hartford
Norris / Morris, Minn., 1877-04-03: aerolite fell on the farm of Hon. R. M. Richardson, seen by Mrs. Baldwin; farmer found a hot 4-inch stone
Bowling Green, Ky., 1877-06-10: stone fell within 10-15 ft of a boy, struck a tree with a cannon-like report
Monticello, Jones Co., Iowa, autumn 1877: fragment fell in Joseph Clark's garden, hissing hot
near Salem, N.C., 1877-11-10: meteor exploded, pieces fell and were buried
Mr. Rawlett's place, 15 mi north of Dallas, Tex., March 1878: saw flame, felt shock, stone fell
6 mi north of Jackson, Tenn. (Madison Co.), April 1878: stone fell in a corn field, clear sky
Surry Co., N.C., May 1878: 20-lb aerolite fell in a man's yard
Sedalia, Mo., June 1878: meteor struck the eaves of Judge Sloan's house on Sixth St.
near Surrounded Hill, Prairie Co., Ark., June 1879: 40-lb stone fell
Rockford, Ill., 1879: 300-lb meteor found on a farm (find?)
Osawatomie, Kan., 1893-04-08: aerolite injured the John Brown statue; analyzed by U.S. Assayer Joplin
near Oroville, Butte Co., Cal.: large meteorite seen to fall years ago, searched for by the Academy of Sciences, found 1893
Wenas valley, North Yakima, Wash.: fell 1890-11-11, location marked by Richard Lisk, dug up Oct 1893 before a crowd
Hooper / Fremont, Neb., April 1911: meteor fell in Mrs. Mary Stuck's yard, buried 5 ft, grass burned; dug out; Prof. Mohler obtained half and found it matches known meteorites
same event as S499 (Hooper, Neb., 1911)
Tule mountain near Doyle, Lassen Co., Cal., 1911-05-26: massive meteor struck, shock felt 30 miles
John Gullickson farm, Washington Island, Wis., 1914: 103-lb meteorite fell; examined by experts, valued at $1,000, purchased (buyer in article)
near Lake Plantagenet, Minn., 1914: Henry Rockensock saw a luminous body bury itself 15 rods from the house; 9-lb object recovered
Thos. Milloy's yard (N.D.), 1914-11-06: 50-lb stone buried 4-5 ft
near Jonesboro, Ill., 1914: A. V. Cook saw a meteorite fall and donated it (listed among gifts at a board meeting)
Webb Co., Tex., Dec 1916: burning meteor fragment through a ranch-house roof set a mattress afire; named witnesses
Virginia, Dec 1916: stone that killed a horse after a brilliant meteor; piece sent for examination
